articles.title: 9/11 vets: Do politicians take the decision to go to war seriously?
articles.description: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. Service and sacrifice cannot be neatly separated, especially when the military has become an instrument of statecraft, diplomacy, humanitarian assistance, and lethal force whose deployment increasingly depends less on congressional authorization than on the decisions of a single president. articles.title: Scorned Trump boots Rwanda, South Africa from trade deal
articles.description: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). This decision comes down to issues that have little to do with the act itself, nor even really with trade between the United States and these countries. Rather, in both cases, their removal from AGOA serves as an act of retribution from a president unhappy with their governments’ policies on domestic or regional issues. But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. The preferential trade agreement — originally signed into law in 2000 by President Bill Clinton and most recently renewed in September for two additional years — provides duty-free access for over 7,000 goods to the U.S. market for qualifying sub-Saharan countries. The study , from Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, followed students at 4,600 schools from the 2021-22 through the 2025-26 school years. Strict bans - lockable Yondr-style pouches, phones stored centrally, or phones kept off campus altogether - raised annual achievement growth by about 0.01 standard deviations , roughly half of what students have been losing each year since smartphones went mainstream. "She had been knowingly giving him secret information. The reason she did it is because she thought he was in love with her. The press appears focused on hot topics like AI and affordability policies. But another item that could be on Democrats' agenda - and has received almost no media attention - may have an even greater impact on the nation's future. For the better part of the last two decades, far-left activists have pushed the idea of abolishing the Electoral College, not through the obvious route of a constitutional amendment but instead through the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) . The proposal attempts to undermine the Constitution by having states pledge their electors to the winner of the national popular vote, regardless of how the states voted. The compact, however, would take effect only when enough states to represent a majority of the Electoral College agree to it. That's what makes the results of the 2026 election so important. articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. articles.title: I’m really hurt that my parents didn’t give me a 40th birthday gift | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.description: You feel overlooked, but your parents’ disappointing behaviour does not necessarily mean they don’t love you I turned 40 a few years ago . For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). articles.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
articles.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

articles.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
articles.description: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples. Cont

articles.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
articles.description: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. articles.title: Is this Britain’s most beautiful bus journey? The Welsh service that beats the train hands down
articles.description: A new coach service between Holyhead in the north and Carmarthen in the south offers a thrilling glimpse of west Wales, from mountain peaks to pretty seafronts – and it knocks half an hour off the journey As anyone who has ever tried to catch a train from north to south Wales will know, it’s quite the adventure, and by adventure, I mean chore. You leave Wales, dip into England and then back into Wales to complete the journey. The fastest “Marches” route, which includes stops in Chester, Crewe and Shrewsbury, takes about five and a half hours and costs about £105, depending on your ticket. There are lots of reasons for this: mid-Wales has some challenging topography; the old rail networks, before the Beeching cuts, predominantly bled outwards, transporting slate, coal and steel to distant ports and markets. Last month, all that changed. Just not in the way you probably imagine. Continue reading...

articles.title: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes
articles.description: As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here • Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge. India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities. Continue reading...

articles.title: Don’t buy new tech this Black Friday: expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops
articles.description: Tech on its last legs? Refurbished can be the cheaper, greener option. Here’s how to choose well and avoid the pitfalls • How to make your phone last longer • The best sustainable Black Friday deals Even if you do your best to avoid it, it’s hard to escape the noise of retailers offering implausible-seeming Black Friday discounts on desirable technology. What they won’t be so keen to highlight is the huge environmental cost that comes from feeding the capitalist beast year on year, given what an obvious sales vibe-killer it would be. While the best approach for the planet is to opt out completely and observe the alternative holiday of Buy Nothing Day instead, such an approach can prove self-defeating for your finances in the long term. If you shop smart on Black Friday and avoid the lure of impulse buys, it’s a good time to stock up on the things you need at lower prices than the rest of the year. Continue reading...

articles.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
articles.description: The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’ ‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.” On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers .” Continue reading...

articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed und

articles.title: After Eight: the story of Satpal Ram - documentary
articles.description: It is 40 years since a racially charged attack at a curry house led to Satpal Ram’s conviction for murder, but today Britain’s post-pub curry culture still has a dark side. Ram spent 24 years in prison before a global campaign for justice, led by bands including Asian Dub Foundation and Primal Scream, secured his release from prison. His case raises crucial questions about the UK’s ongoing struggle for racial equality Continue reading...

articles.title: The 45 best Secret Santa gifts in the UK for £15 or less – tried and tested for 2026
articles.description: From grippy socks and posh condiments to beautiful stationery and accessories, these affordable Christmas presents are anything but naff • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 Secret Santa is an amazing concept to reduce the amount of gifts you feel obliged to buy, but I find it can result in quite a bit of tat. Resist the urge to buy a joke gift – often instant landfill – and use your budget to get your recipient something useful, or that feels quite treat-y. I’m assuming for this guide that the rules of Secret Santa are that you know who your recipient is – they just don’t know who the gift is from. That is helpful as you can tailor it to their tastes and hobbies. If it’s blind both ways, food is always well received, and socks – while a Christmas cliche – are something everyone wants a new pair of (just get the best you can afford, not, as one of my family used to do, just restock my black school socks). Continue reading...

articles.title: Get vaccinated, don’t vape – and moisturise liberally! 10 doctors on how to avoid and treat winter ailments
articles.description: The nights are drawing in, the temperature is dropping, festive overindulgence is on the horizon and it’s easy to get run down. Here’s some expert advice to help you safely through the season Winter can be a challenging time, with bad weather, dark evenings, horrible bugs circulating, plus plenty of opportunities for overindulging. How can we avoid getting run down? Doctors share their tips for surviving the season, from saunas to screen blockers, light boxes to apples. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘In the end, nothing happened’: how Reform’s Doge-style crackdown fell flat
articles.description: Party promised a Musk-inspired blitz at councils in England, but research shows it has failed to cut harder or faster than comparable local authorities When Reform UK secured a historic breakthrough in the May local elections last year, it was – according to the party leader, Nigel Farage – time for the UK to emulate Donald Trump and make sweeping local government cuts. At the time, the US president had enlisted the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, to run his “department of government efficiency” (Doge). During a 16-week blitz at the heart of the US government , Musk caused chaos, fired tens of thousands of workers and gutted USAID. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best Christmas baubles in the UK: 26 quirky decorations, from a velvet turnip to a Suffragette mouse
articles.description: Bored of red and gold? This year’s tree trimmings are felted, beaded and handmade – and they’re all glitter-free • The best artificial Christmas trees – tested Baubles: every time we think we’ve reached peak wackiness, we’re proved wrong the following year. On the menu for 2026 are food and drink ornaments, with everything from Guinness to gildas; felt animals with imaginative personalities, jobs and political agendas (see the suffragette mouse); and retro-inspired ornaments, including a cute gramophone. And we couldn’t resist a handmade decoration paying tribute to the late, great Amy Winehouse. Here are our favourites, and they’re all glitter-free. *** Continue reading...

articles.title: Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial
articles.description: Exclusive: Jury was never told that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was barred from practising over concerns for patients’ safety A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial over fears he posed a risk to their safety. Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that the British nurse had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told. Continue reading...

articles.title: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January
articles.description: Government under pressure to help households as increase would add £443 to average annual dual-fuel bill Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers Tell us: are you shopping around for a better deal? UK inflation rises to 3.6% Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households. The government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is likely to rise by 26% early next year, equivalent to adding £443 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, in one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The sea washed away trees, then a whole row of houses. I knew it was time to get out’ – This is climate breakdown
articles.description: She noticed the trees going first. Slowly she understood that the sea was going to take the whole village. This is Guadalupe Cobos Pacheco’s story Location: El Bosque, Mexico Disaster: Sea encroachment The fishing village of El Bosque was the first community in Mexico to be recogni sed as climate-displaced. The inhabitants were moved in 2023 . By then, coastal erosion and flooding had already taken many of the homes. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
articles.description: He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original ‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.” Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles rel

articles.title: Nicola Coughlan on her favourite noodles, getting rejected from drama school and I Am Helen
articles.description: What does Lady Whistledown eat when nobody's watching?  This week on Comfort Eating, Siobhán McSweeney is joined by the brilliant Nicola Coughlan, star of Derry Girls and Bridgerton, for a seriously fun catch-up involving comfort food, childhood nostalgia and some VERY questionable food combinations. Nicola brings her ultimate comfort food to the table: think fusion - or perhaps it’s confusion. There's also Diet Coke mixed with pickle juice (yes, really), stories about growing up in Galway, and her Supermac's Gold Card. Plus, Nicola reflects on her journey into acting, drama school rejection, the early struggles of making it in London and how life changed after Derry Girls and Bridgerton. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel
articles.description: The documentary has triggered fierce backlash, but by exposing the army’s conduct in Gaza it’s proved impossible to ignore It was on Yom Kippur this year that Nadav Weiman first sensed the documentary NAZA was having a significant impact in Israel – despite the fact that back in September, when the Jewish festival fell, barely a handful of Israelis had seen the film. NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and will stream for free on its website in early December, depicts 24 army intelligence officers interviewed anonymously on rooftops across Tel Aviv. They talk about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza over the past three years, and the secret signoff system employed by Israel’s military. More than 1.5 million people have already seen it in cinemas and its Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have picked up a roster of prestigious awards. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet, amid a severe backlash. Continue reading...

articles.title: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle
articles.description: Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style. Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “ gjak ” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Narrators don’t shy away from descriptions of how “shrapnel sliced [them] up like a fillet – eyes, teeth, ripped off half a jaw”.

articles.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
articles.description: Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. Continue reading...

articles.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
articles.description: National Gallery, London Bringing together all the pioneering master’s portraits for the first time reveals the way he clinically preserved monsters, merchants – even his wife – like flies in amber Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean? The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck. The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on w

articles.title: Cosimo I de’Medici review – up close and personal with a Renaissance godfather
articles.description: Wallace Collection, London A sword, a wine cooler, a dazzling fresco … only a museum with such a copious store of treasures could put on a display this rich without having to borrow Mounting a “store-cupboard” exhibition – choosing items from existing collections to make a new, contained display – can be a cheap and easy way for a museum to make something out of its existing resources, without the faff of securing loans or collaborating across the industry. In the case of the Wallace Collection, however, the store cupboard is so embarrassingly rich and diverse that strong displays such as this on Cosimo I de’Medici can be drawn from only a handful of its objects. The 19th-century collection of Sir Richard Wallace holds a notable number of medieval objects, but their display can seem – at least to contemporary eyes – like a cacophony of applied arts, armour and paintings, not to mention a ton of gilt. This Medici display is part of a new enterprise drawing out histories from the noise for singular focus, sensibly repurposing what was once the cloakroom (a previously wasted bit of prime real estate) as a new dedicated space. Continue reading...

articles.title: A moment that changed me: the tomato pasta that became an obsession – and helped me lead a better life
articles.description: At a restaurant in Italy in 2022, every forkful of my meal made my eyes close and mouth water. For four years since, I have tried to recreate this dish. The pursuit has finally made me a proper vegetarian I’ve ostensibly been vegetarian for 13 years and, in that time, I’ve eaten a lot of meat. My mum used to leave out the last bit of lamb madras, with a wink, then loudly announce that she was going to bed. I have accidentally found myself in KFC at midnight, hood up, drunk, looking both ways and asking for a Bargain Bucket. My partner once came home early from a night out and caught me red-handed, in bed with McDonald’s Chicken Selects. Such incidents were infrequent moments of weakness and, after the fact, I was always racked with guilt. But for most of my vegetarian life, I had felt a certain emptiness; a gaping meat-shaped hole in my heart and stomach. Then I ate a bowl of pasta. It was 2022 and an Italian university friend, Mattia, invited me to Tuscany. I spent four days with his lovely family, in the rolling verdant hills, with fireflies and fallow deer keeping us company, drinking vernaccia and talking of books and art and poetry. But none of that matters, not even a bit. Al

articles.title: How to deal with a class difference in friendships? Make fun of your privileged friends
articles.description: Lasting cross-class friendships involve routinely ‘taking the piss’ out of the more privileged party, research by the LSE shows Routinely “taking the piss” out of more privileged friends is one of the main ways people cope with a class difference in their friendships, research has found. Cross-class friendships are widespread and mutually beneficial, a study by the London School of Economics showed, but a class gap can still pose an “omnipresent threat” to friendships. Continue reading...

articles.title: Life insurance: what is it and do you need it?
articles.description: It could protect you and your family in the event of death or accident – and in some cases it costs no more than a TV streaming service No one wants to spend time imagining the worst thing that could happen, and perhaps that is why about 60% of UK adults have no life insurance, or why more people have pet insurance than have income protection for if they become too sick to work. However, there are certain milestones in life, such as having children or taking on a mortgage, that focus the mind on what might happen if things do go wrong. How would your family manage if you or your partner died? How would you cover the mortgage if you had an accident and couldn’t work? Continue reading...

articles.title: Pill that mimics Viagra can slow Alzheimer’s progression, study suggests
articles.description: Experts call trial results of medication that slowed cognitive decline by almost a third ‘very promising’ A pill that mimics Viagra by relaxing blood vessels and increasing blood flow to the brain can slow cognitive decline in people with Alzheimer’s disease by almost a third, a global study suggests. Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, a condition that is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050. There is currently no cure. Continue reading...

articles.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
articles.description: A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.” It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy
articles.description: From icy squirts to bed-bouncing vibrations, erotic hockey drama Heated Rivalry just got even raunchier in ‘extreme sensory’ 4DX cinema screenings. But one scene proved too much – even for the super fans I’m in the cinema foyer when I first spot them: hockey jerseys. Lots of them. “I’ve no idea what to expect!” giggles Chloe, who is wearing a black and yellow “Rozanov” jersey. Like me, she has never been to a 4DX screening before – but when Cineworld announced it would be showing episodes five and six of queer hockey drama Heated Rivalry in the novel format, she booked tickets immediately. “I actually had tickets for the 2D screening, but cancelled them for this,” she says. Over the last two weeks, Heated Rivalry fans have been treated to big screen marathons of Jacob Tierney’s hit TV show, based on Rachel Reid’s bestselling book series, Game Changers. But 4DX is next level. The “extreme sensory” cinema technology is usually deployed for high-octane action flicks – films with epic battles or chase sequences. Still, with Cineworld offering the opportunity to “immerse yourself in the motion, wind, water [and] scent” of major league hockey’s raunchiest fictional romance, who could res

articles.title: EU ‘to close door’ to talks on long-term UK ties until Burnham has decided on Brexit
articles.description: Diplomats say piecemeal approach of resets is coming to an end and Europe wants clarity on whether Britain wants to reverse its exit The EU will shut the door to discussions with Andy Burnham about the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc until the government has decided whether it wants to proceed with reversing Brexit, diplomats have said. European capitals are also warning they have reached the end of the line for piecemeal “reset” summits with the UK and want the prime minister to focus on his next steps domestically before they proceed. Continue reading...

articles.title: World ‘held hostage by oil mafia’, says Panama minister at Cop 31
articles.description: Key issues unresolved as summit enters final days, with 30 countries signed up to forge fossil fuel treaty separate to UN process The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister has warned, as key issues remain unresolved in the final days of the UN Cop31 climate summit . “We are in love with our kidnappers,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, at a press conference to announce 30 countries were now signed up to forge a new fossil fuel treaty, separate to the UN process. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.” Continue reading...

articles.title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot
articles.description: Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different. Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
articles.description: A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies “Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement. The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
articles.description: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded. But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “ two-tier policing ” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them. Do you have an opinion on the issues raise

articles.title: Why Palantir’s health tech is not the right fit for the NHS | Letter
articles.description: The US firm’s health data system is based on an insurance model of healthcare, not the patient-centred universal service we have in Britain, says Prof Caroline Mitchell The news that NHS England may have overstated the benefits of Palantir for improving efficiency will surprise few frontline clinicians ( NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools, 12 November ) Too often, global digital policy assumes that software designed for the fragmented, insurance-based US healthcare system can simply be adapted to a universal public service elsewhere. A legitimate concern is that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature in the NHS context, having been developed primarily for a very different US healthcare system. Continue reading...

articles.title: Blaming Ofsted inspectors for the system is unfair | Letters
articles.description: Inspectors and educators alike have been placed under even greater pressure year after year, says Helen Kenny As national officer for the FDA, the union representing a large number of His Majesty’s Inspectors (HMIs), I read Simon Jenkins’ piece with great interest ( Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve, 13 November ). Jenkins dismisses the work of HMIs as merely a “sniff” of the air and a stroll back to Whitehall, showing a lack of knowledge about their role. HMIs are former school leaders, with a deep knowledge and dedication to educating children and young people. They are as far from the typical civil servant (if there is such a thing) that it is possible to get, and in any case are not based in Whitehall. Jenkins does at least suggest an alternative approach, unlike some who are calling for the abolition of Ofsted, but I really question whether he has thought it through. Parents value the provision of inspection, and most educators agree that assessments are fair – independent YouGov polling showed that 74% of educators believed their most recent inspection was accurate. Continue reading...

articles.title: What stops us building the houses Britain needs | Letters
articles.description: Emeritus professor Simon Price , Smart Growth UK’s Jon Reeds and former Labour council leader Steve Siddon respond to a column by John Harris John Harris points out the utter inadequacy of Labour’s housing plans, despite Andy Burnham’s passionate advocacy for new social housing ( Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream?, 15 November ). And everyone agrees that we need many more houses. So what’s holding us back? The problem lies in the fiscal rules. At first sight this is puzzling, as borrowing to invest is explicitly allowed (as opposed to borrowing to cover current expenditure). The explanation is the future debt target. Any capital investment increases public debt, and there is a binding debt-to-GDP ratio at the arbitrary and relatively close forecast horizon. Continue reading...

articles.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
articles.description: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place ( BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November ). The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies. Continue reading...

articles.title: More gas storage is at risk. What’s the government plan for secure supplies?
articles.description: SSE’s threat to close a big storage facility in Yorkshire highlights successive governments’ failures to build a strategy and safeguard supplies Labour faces double blow over UK fossil fuel projects For those who followed the many months of government dithering over whether to approve production at the Jackdaw gasfield off the coast of Aberdeen, Scotland, there was a treat on social media this week. It was the sight of Michael Shanks, energy minister, almost dancing a jig of delight as the first output from Jackdaw flowed into the national gas network. “It will increase domestic production and further boost our energy security during the transition to electrification and decarbonisation,” he declared . Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Cherubino’s in’t’ cupboard’: Mozart via Bradford and Bollywood is a blast
articles.description: Bradford Arts Centre Ian McMillan’s south Yorkshire language version of The Marriage of Figaro sets the opera in 1970s Bradford. Indian classical instruments join to the reworked score in this high-energy, low-budget and hugely enjoyable take ‘This will be better than Barnsley FC,” I overheard the poet, broadcaster and professional Yorkshireman Ian McMillan assuring a friend ahead of curtain-up on his dialect adaptation of Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro. “Everything’s better than Barnsley FC.” I don’t know much about League One football, I admit, but this high-energy, low-budget production directed by Alex Chisholm for Bradford Opera Festival punches far above its weight and could definitely survive less self-deprecating comparisons. Continue reading...

articles.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
articles.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green mo

articles.title: The best TVs in the UK for every home and screen size, tested
articles.description: Not sure which TV is right for you? articles.title: How to turn the dregs of an instant coffee jar into a brilliant vegan cake – recipe | Waste not
articles.description: Instant coffee granules are a great ingredient in baking, as shown in this sponge given extra depth from roast walnuts and cardamom-infused milk It might taste subpar in the cup, but instant coffee is a great baking ingredient. Being dehydrated, it provides an intense coffee flavour without adding extra liquid, which often upsets the balance of a recipe. I don’t drink instant coffee myself, and the dregs of the jar we always seem to have at the back of the cupboard tend to grow old and stick together. They’re still good to use, though, and can be chipped off or even dissolved in the jar, if need be. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records

Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. articles.title: Dashing through the snow: 10 of the UK’s best Christmas train rides
articles.description: Heritage railways will soon be steaming into action, with special departures offering winter landscapes, seasonal goodies and a chance to meet Father Christmas Red tablecloths, festive decor and tartan upholstered carriage seats bring the yuletide vibe onboard Strathspey Railway’s Elf Express. From your first-class carriage of either a steam-hauled or heritage diesel engine, you will be served sandwiches and cakes from traditional tiered plates, washed down with hot drinks and fizz. Santa and his elves will visit your carriage with presents for children, otherwise sit back and enjoy the woodland and moorland scenery of rural Speyside on this 20-mile round-trip (lasting about 1 hour and 40 minutes) between Aviemore and Broomhill. Weekends and select weekdays until 24 December, £260 for four people . Continue reading...

articles.title: Guarding Stars review – Leighton Meester is a delight in fizzy Netflix holiday romance
articles.description: As a female bodyguard protecting an A-list star, the Gossip Girl actor shines in Christmas movie a cut above the competition Though it is my personal opinion that Christmas should not begin until after Thanksgiving, I am pleased to say that we already have at least one treat in Netflix’s holiday movie assembly line: Guarding Stars, starring Leighton Meester as a frosty bodyguard tasked with protecting Jared Padalecki’s movie star at, of all places, his family’s Montana ranch, falls on the fizzy side of seasonal fluff. Good holiday movies are an exercise in knowing silliness, and so it is a relief when the first 10 minutes of this movie, directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum, strikes the rare December balance between hearth-like warmth (the twinkle in Meester’s chocolate eyes when her Hannah Brooks lands a verbal punch) and complete lunacy (she lands that punch in an argument with her ex about … cuddling … literally seconds after thwarting an assassination attempt in Times Square). As a homespun band of hot would-be cowboys later drawl at a Christmas parade in “Montana” (Canada, per usual): “Christmas is back, y’all.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Mike Lynch’s superyacht had unidentified vulnerability to high winds, report finds
articles.description: Bayesian, which sank off Sicily killing seven including tech tycoon, had not been fully assessed, say investigators The superyacht Bayesian, which sank in a storm off Sicily killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter, was vulnerable to knockdown but crew were not aware as it had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down, the final report from the UK’s Marine Accident Investigations Branch (MAIB) has said. articles.description: Chataigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), which was painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-impressionist A Vincent van Gogh masterpiece sold for a record-breaking $190.4m (£144.9m, A$285m) on Wednesday after a dispute between the seller and the heirs of a previous Jewish owner who sold it in the Nazi era, Sotheby’s said. Chataigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), which was painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-impressionist and became the most expensive work auctioned off so far this season. articles.title: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable
articles.description: Nathan Fielder’s intense close-range study of fraudster Elizabeth Holmes is as gripping as any thriller • This review contains spoilers Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes . It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger. Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
articles.description: Like Russell Brand, my father was put on a pedestal by the media, despite a history of troubling, misogynistic comments. Meanwhile, my mother suffered through years of appalling treatment Even though decades have passed, part of me feels I should not be telling this story. Not because it isn’t true, but because telling makes it real. And the reality is very hard to bear. I was a young child at home in Whitechapel, east London, when my mother came into my bedroom, which was next to my parents’, and told me that my father had raped her. He had gone off to work and I was too young to fully understand what the words meant – perhaps seven or eight – and I remember being angry with her for upsetting life again, as she had done before, when she suddenly came to me at the top of the stairs and told me that they would “have to part” and that would mean taking me away with her. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
articles.description: Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors? Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the p

articles.title: Nothing but highlights: is Power Slap the sport we deserve?
articles.description: Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place. It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back. Continue reading...

articles.title: Want to shop more sustainably this Black Friday? The best UK deals on eco-friendly products we love

Approach it with care, though, and Black Friday is a good opportunity to buy eco-friendly products that might normally stretch your budget. articles.title: Outages, spies, and trillion-dollar IPOs: is this our AI future? – Stateside with Kai and Carter
articles.description: It has been a wild few weeks in the world of tech. First, Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, forced an unimaginable leadership change at Nvidia – arguably the most consequential company in AI development. Then, chaos erupted as a rolling set of IT outages disrupted flights, banking, tech companies and the federal government. And now, Anthropic is blowing minds with a trillion-dollar IPO – one of the largest in stock market history. The Atlantic’s tech writer Charlie Warzel tells Kai Wright that these events are linked: they’re all examples of the ways in which we shoulder unprecedented risk today, in order to bet on AI’s future reward. It’s a convoluted logic that keeps the AI race speeding forward, no matter how many warning signs it blows past. Charlie Warzel is also host of the Atlantic’s podcast Galaxy Brain . Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier
articles.description: The actor’s latest roles see him go from a delivery guy on £40 a day to the notorious crypto scammer who stole more than $10bn. His sympathies are clear: ‘I wasn’t brought up to care about money,’ he says In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’” Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning , ab

articles.title: Bank your stolen cash, bring a change of clothes, go easy on the bloodshed: 15 tips for playing Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: There’s a vast amount to absorb in Leonida, but these pointers will rev up your criminal engines and allow you to better enjoy the ride Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? Leonida is so huge as to be overwhelming and in the opening hours, the game bombards you with tonnes of info that you will inevitably forget. But I’ve done nothing but play this game for weeks and I’m here to help. Here’s what I wished I’d known at the start Walk faster. I found that Jason and Lucia walk incredibly slowly. If you go into the options menu, you can select “fast walk” as the default walking speed, which sped them up just a little without ruining the pace or atmosphere of the game. While you’re in there, you can also customise plenty of other things, including controls and button mapping. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trance, prog synths, guttural screaming: Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages is the year’s wildest electronic album
articles.description: (Warp) The Milan producer revisits his youth as a straight-edge punk fan voyeuristically dabbling in rave – and finds a thrilling interzone between both genres The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”. A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012’s Quantum Jelly and 2014’s Superimpositions featured what Senni called “pointillistic trance”, spinning the i
