articles.title: Ram through datacentres no one wants and hope the AI bubble never bursts: that’s the UK’s growth plan | George Monbiot
articles.description: The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns , advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for moratoria on new datacentres, tech

articles.title: Teachers want to prepare pupils for post-16 life. This is why it’s so difficult | Lola Okolosie
articles.description: I welcome Alan Milburn’s call for schools to focus more on students’ potential beyond exams. Yet I must ask: where is the money? At 16, life should feel like a path leading to endless opportunities. That is at least the carrot dangled in front of young people to motivate them through the gruelling years of exam preparation. “Your life starts now,” their teachers all but tell them. And though for the vast majority that is true, there is a cohort who are forced to accept that the bright futures they were promised are beyond their reach. They are the nearly one million young people aged between 16 and 24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets). Alan Milburn’s second report on the nation’s Neets places schools at the heart of the solution. It proposes that schools should be judged not only on grades but also whether pupils continue their post-16 journey into further education or work. Technical education, it also argues, must be regarded with the same gravitas as the academic. Most people working in education won’t argue with this rationale. As ever, the sticking point is how it is to be funded. Lola Okolosie is an English teacher and writer Continue reading...

articles.title: This year, the Greens have reshaped British politics. Now we need party systems to match that influence | Caroline Lucas
articles.description: Without Zack Polanski and Hannah Spencer, we might still be stuck with Keir Starmer. But after some difficult weeks, our party needs an overhaul Caroline Lucas is co-chair of the cross-party campaign group Compass and a former Green MP In the aftermath of some difficult weeks for the Greens, one encouraging response has particularly stood out for me: the widespread agreement across progressive politics that the UK is better for having a strong Green party. One that will hold other parties to account for their delivery on social and environmental justice and that will put issues on the political agenda that other parties won’t. From Rosebank to wealth taxes and ending arms sales to Israel, Greens are stretching the Overton window so that the gap narrows between what’s necessary and what’s currently deemed politically acceptable. As we increasingly win more council seats, assembly members, mayors and MPs we are able, at all levels of government, to help restore the natural world, tackle climate breakdown and challenge the economic framework of neoliberalism that has governed us for too long, help restore the natural world and tackle climate breakdown. Caroline Lucas is co-chair of th

articles.title: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew
articles.description: Why do rich powerful men love golf? Ultimately the sport exists in a world where the politics is assumed to be settled Farewell, then, LIV Golf. As its original figurehead Greg Norman once so delicately put it, albeit in a slightly different context: we’ve all made mistakes, you learn from those mistakes, and you move forward. Forward – in LIV’s case – to bankruptcy court and the start of liquidation proceedings some time in January 2027. And not without a certain irony, in the sense that Norman’s cherished project, established over a cacophony of human rights concerns, ended up getting dismembered and terminated on the orders of the Saudi government. Life moves on you pretty fast. Perhaps the funniest part of LIV’s protracted demise – unless you count the television viewing figures – has been the last seven months, after Saudi Arabia abruptly pulled the plug on the seemingly abundant flow of money that had fuelled its astonishing rise. Suddenly LIV’s chief executive, Scott O’Neil, was forced to take his begging bowl up and down midtown Manhattan, panhandling for change, drawing up entirely conceptual revenue forecasts, pretending for all the world that this was an actual, real-lif

articles.title: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland
articles.description: In laying a trap for himself, the PM could derail his longer-term ambition of revisiting Brexit This week’s UK-EU summit may, one day, be seen as the start of the UK’s long march back towards the EU. Andy Burnham’s much-anticipated first meeting with EU chiefs in Brussels on Friday will be used to unveil a suite of detailed agreements to improve trade and economic cooperation, before the Prime Minister kickstarts his longer term “national conversation” about a much closer form of political and economic relationship with the EU. This, as Burnham signalled in a speech on Monday night , could well culminate in Labour’s next election manifesto abandoning the party’s famous red lines, and proposing an application for EU membership. For pro-Europeans, this must read like a fever dream. Just four months ago, when Burnham took office, such a bold offer on Europe from the Labour party seemed implausible. But while Burnham has certainly reinvigorated the Brexit debate, he will have to move carefully to avoid storing up trouble for himself down the road. There is a risk that Burnham will come to be seen as someone who over-promises and under-delivers on Europe – and, in doing so, halts the gr

articles.title: Measles has come raging back in the US. Robert F Kennedy Jr should be impeached | Judith Levine
articles.description: He is responsible for the health of the American people. On his watch, thousands have become seriously ill At least 11 Americans have died of measles since January 2025 – the month before Robert F Kennedy Jr became secretary of Health and Human Services. One of Friday’s victims was a child, in Wisconsin, where a baby died of measles the week before. Pennsylvania has not disclosed the age of the other person. Continue reading...

articles.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
articles.description: We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice. Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of Dem

articles.title: Mauricio Pochettino calls for Manchester United to show no fear against Liverpool
articles.description: New head coach’s first game is at Anfield on Sunday ‘We are going there with the idea to win and be brave’ Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start. United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach will not accept nerves. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and will bring those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick. Continue reading...

articles.title: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’
articles.description: Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under-21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one. Time to talk, so let’s start with tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and rec

articles.title: From training clips to thirst traps: why athletes are turning to OnlyFans
articles.description: A professional sports career does not guarantee wealth. And a growing number of athletes are turning to alternative streams of income “I’m sick and tired of it.” Bart Swings tossed his jacket behind him. It was August 2025, the Winter Olympics were less than six months away, and the Belgian Olympic champion’s injured knee was not getting better. The clip, profanity and all, later ran on the Belgian evening news along with the weather and the football. But the injury update didn’t come from an interview – it was broadcast on the speed skater’s OnlyFans channel. The subscription site, best known for porn dudes, cam girls and dubiously horny couples, has quietly assembled one of the stranger rosters in professional sport. The list, about 285 athletes deep, includes Olympic speed skaters and rowers, tennis players, surfers and golfers. And, despite its racy reputation, many of the athletes on OnlyFans are not putting out adult content. Continue reading...

articles.title: England’s ‘fresh’ rookies roll on to Australia T20s as Test stars depart early
articles.description: Root, Duckett, Archer, Atkinson and Baker head home McCullum: ‘Brook has an unbelievable tactical brain’ Fresh from turning over Australia in the 50-over leg of this tour, England’s attention now turns to the Twenty20s that start on Saturday. Five players jet home for a swift breather before the Tests in South Africa, with fresh-faced rookies coming in. Joe Root, Ben Duckett, Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker were the men heading for the departure lounge, while captain Harry Brook and wicketkeeper Jordan Cox will leave after the fourth of the five T20Is on 29 November. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Closing the door halts growth’: Liv Apps on PWR’s international appeal – and pruning the Red Roses
articles.description: Saracens and Canada scrum-half believes having fewer overseas players in England’s top tier would be a backwards step both for her and the wider game Liv Apps understands only too well the benefits of playing in Premiership Women’s Rugby (PWR), so when challenging the views of the Red Roses’ head coach, John Mitchell, it comes from the heart. According to the Saracens and Canada scrum-half, limiting the international talent pool in England’s elite division would halt the growth of the game, or even dilute the PWR’s potency. “For us Canadians, it is amazing to have the PWR because we don’t have a league at home. But then also what the Canadians and the other internationals bring to the England players, we all make each other better.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
articles.description: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly It’s injury time at the Emirates on the 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Spurs. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and on to the post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs fans before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it. But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Race for the Fifa presidency: lineup revealed to challenge Gianni Infantino
articles.description: Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima are both standing But Ramon Vega fails to get the necessary backing Fifa has confirmed that Gianni Infantino will face challenges from Philippe Diallo of France and Japan’s Kozo Tashima in March’s presidential election. The president of the French Football Federation and honorary president of the Japan Football Association submitted nomination letters with endorsements from five member associations by Wednesday night’s midnight CET deadline. The former Switzerland and Tottenham defender Ramon Vega has not met that threshold, despite repeatedly saying he would stand. Continue reading...

articles.title: World marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir banned for three years over doping
articles.description: Three leading Kenyan distance runners all sanctioned Jepchirchir also won the Olympic gold medal in Tokyo The reigning world marathon champion, Peres Jepchirchir, has been hit with a three-year ban for EPO on a dismal day for Kenyan distance running, with two other leading distance athletes from the country also being punished for doping. The 33-year-old Jepchirchir, who won Olympic and world gold in Tokyo in 2021 and 2025 respectively, had her ban reduced by a year after she decided not to challenge the results of a blood test taken before winning the Sydney marathon in August . Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I see comments every day’: Sonay Kartal’s fightback against injury and online abuse
articles.description: British tennis star has bounced back after six months out but wants more to be done about vitriol aimed at players Sonay Kartal believes the vitriolic abuse and threats that she and her fellow players receive after every match have become an unavoidable part of her job. “Unfortunately, it’s something that comes with the sport,” the British No 2 says. “I don’t really have a choice to not deal with it. Obviously, it’s not a good thing to have and as a player, win or lose, you’re seeing those things. Continue reading...

articles.title: Danish MPs approve Greenland security pact with US
articles.description: Danish foreign minister says deal ‘removes all uncertainty’ over territory but warns trust in US needs rebuilding Europe live – latest updates The Danish parliament has unanimously approved a new Arctic security pact between Greenland, Denmark and the US in what it is hoped will mark a new chapter in relations, months after Donald Trump’s threats to invade the largely autonomous territory. The deal, which was signed by the US president and the prime ministers of Greenland and Denmark, Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Mette Frederiksen, in September after months of talks, updates a 1951 defence agreement to give the US underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system. Continue reading...

articles.title: Anthropic to float on the stock market today as it raises $81bn in record IPO – business live
articles.description: Rolling coverage of Anthropic’s IPO, and the latest economic and financial news Anthropic needs to grow into its $1.5tn valuation, argues Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB: Anthropic’s triumphant IPO and its trillion dollar plus valuation is more typical of a mature company that has a history of strong fundamentals. Anthropic could not be more different. It has generated strong revenue growth, but only in the short term, added to this, it is still unprofitable. Anthropic is another major tech company that requires investors to have a lot of faith about the future generation of revenues based on technology that will change the world. It seems like plenty are willing to give it that faith, and it is having a huge impact on the broader market today. Continue reading...

articles.title: Edinburgh festival to mark 80-year anniversary with longest ever season
articles.description: Running for more than four weeks, 2027 festival features staging of play starring Ewan McGregor and Alan Cumming The Edinburgh international festival is to stage its longest season next year when it marks 80 years since its foundation in the aftermath of the second world war. The festival will run for just over four weeks in August 2027, longer than its customary three weeks, and focus heavily on the role of the arts in unifying cultures and transcending conflict. Continue reading...

articles.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
articles.description: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia. The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions. Continue reading...

articles.title: Weight-loss drugs used in nearly one in 10 homes in Great Britain, study finds
articles.description: About 2.6m adults are taking the drugs, fuelled by the regulator’s approval of the pill versions and a rise in male users At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users than those containing vegetarians and pescatarians combined. About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, according to a survey by Worldpanel by Numerator . Continue reading...

articles.title: Meet Phil, the bar-tailed godwit tracked on a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia
articles.description: Scientists use lightweight tracker to map wading bird’s extraordinary migration from Norfolk to the Arctic and back A bar-tailed godwit called Phil has completed a 6,800-mile journey from Norfolk to Siberia and back again, in the first mapping of the endurance feats of this long-distance migrant. A wading bird not much larger than a pigeon, the bar-tailed godwit is known for making the longest recorded non-stop migratory flight of any bird, with populations that visit Britain spending summers breeding in the Arctic Circle before retreating to the unfrozen wetlands of Britain in winter. Continue reading...

articles.title: Car use in London forecast to rise by 10% in next decade
articles.description: Modelling in draft of 10-year London plan threatens Sadiq Khan’s promises on improving air quality Car use in London will rise by 10% over the next decade with cycling and walking falling as a proportion of trips, according to an official forecast by the city’s mayoralty, putting into doubt Sadiq Khan’s promises on air quality and the environment. Based on projections in the draft version of the latest 10-year London plan , drawn up by the mayor’s office and Transport for London (TfL), road congestion from a growing population would slow buses down, while packed tube services might require stations to close regularly to ease numbers. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tulip Siddiq says she is considering legal action against former Bangladesh leader
articles.description: Former minister, who was sentenced to prison in Bangladesh in her absence, says she was victim of ‘malicious prosecution’ The former minister Tulip Siddiq has said she is considering taking legal action against the former interim leader of Bangladesh over corruption allegations made by his administration led her to resign from the UK government last year. The MP for Hampstead and Highgate, whose aunt Sheikh Hasina was put on trial in absentia over crimes against humanity during her 15 years as prime minister of Bangladesh, was accused of benefiting from the former regime by the authorities in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka. Continue reading...

articles.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
articles.description: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report. In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund ( UNFPA ) published on Thursday. Continue reading...

articles.title: Violent protests and killings in Bangladesh ahead of exiled Sheikh Hasina’s planned return
articles.description: Awami League party called for ⁠nationwide protest on Thursday after the government rejected Hasina’s request for passport Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home ⁠of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence. Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a ​week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support ‌for Hasina’s planned return in December , culminating in a ‌nationwide lockdown on Thursday. Continue reading...

articles.title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
articles.description: UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home. A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera . Continue reading...

articles.title: BAE to slash 1,000 jobs across head office and air business
articles.description: Cuts – which exclude shop floor and aircraft maintenance – prompt calls for more orders to support British defence contractor BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, prompting calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor. The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The abuse I copped was phenomenal’: researchers accuse tobacco companies of intimidation tactics to silence critics
articles.description: Exclusive: Industry tactics are part of ‘deliberate strategy’ to distort evidence and weaken regulation, paper says Prof Charlotta Pisinger, a medical doctor and public health researcher, was speaking to this journalist about her experiences of intimidation by the tobacco industry when another complaint to her employer landed in her inbox. The Danish subsidiary of the tobacco company Philip Morris International (PMI) had just filed a complaint accusing her of breaching the University of Southern Denmark’s research communication standards for media interviews she gave questioning the safety of heated tobacco and vapes and whether PMI really cared about improving health. Continue reading...

articles.title: EDF snaps up 1.3m more customers after Utilita takeover
articles.description: Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier brings account base up to 6m after purchase of pay-as-you-go supplier EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m customer accounts after snapping up the pay-as-you-go supplier Utilita. Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier expects to complete the takeover early next year, adding 1.3m accounts to its customer base and taking on Utilita’s 1,500 staff. The price of the deal was undisclosed. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean?
articles.description: The more you gaze at ​these 10 surviving works, ​with their cryptic inscriptions and even fool’s gold, the more the Flemish master trips you up​ – but being laughed at like this is all part of the glorious pleasure Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings At the Barbican Art Gallery in London, there is an exhibition of some of the white paintings made by the US artist Robert Ryman over 60 years from the 1950s. The paintings are square, because a square is neutral, and he didn’t want viewers associating them with the visual language of landscape or portrait. For Ryman, his paintings resolutely were what they were, which is to say, white paint applied to various surfaces and fixed to the wall. Not “windows” through which one could glimpse another world. At the National Gallery, a couple of miles across town, is an exhibition of 10 works by the 15th-century Flemish painter Jan van Eyck. With one exception – the Arnolfini portrait, which is a one-off in all kinds of ways – they are all A4-size portraits, each angled so that we see more of the left than the right side of their faces. Aside from the likenesses of the people who paid for them in

articles.title: ‘No publicist or manager in sight’: 80s Madonna, unseen and off-duty – in pictures
articles.description: In Madonna Into the Groove: An Intimate Portrait of the Queen of Pop , photographer Ken Regan opens his archive from 1985 to show never-before-seen photographs of the musician. The 160-page hardback showcases Madonna at her most vibrant, captured on a February day in Los Angeles, with accompanying biographical text by journalist Tomás Mier. With the majority of images previously unpublished, the book is a behind-the-scenes look at an artist coming into the peak of her powers Continue reading...

articles.title: TV tonight: survivors from the Bondi beach terror attack share their stories
articles.description: Harrowing accounts of the Hanukah celebration attack in Sydney last December. Plus: Marci Pierre White and Gordon Ramsay reunite. Here’s what to watch this evening 10pm, Channel 4 This harrowing documentary recalls the events of 14 December 2025 when terrorists attacked a Hanukah celebration taking place in Sydney. It’s also a celebration of the courage of the first responders – and of the many people who put their own lives on the line to save those under attack. The survivor testimony and the attack footage make it a difficult watch but it’s a striking one, too. Phil Harrison Continue reading...

articles.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
articles.description: This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing. The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suz

articles.title: ‘Perhaps we are safer not knowing’: a year after his death, Rob Reiner’s JFK assassination book is revealed
articles.description: The late director worked with David Hoffman and Dick Russell on a book about his lifelong fascination with what really happened on 22 November 1963 On 8 December last year, the great director Rob Reiner signed off the prologue for Who Killed JFK? , his book written with David Hoffman and Dick Russell and based on his podcast with Soledad O’Brien. Describing a lifelong fascination with the assassination of John F Kennedy in Dallas on 22 November 1963, and what he saw as the vast conspiracy to cover up who really killed the 35th president, Reiner wrote: “Maybe, people don’t truly want an answer. Perhaps we are safer not knowing … Well, I’m done being safe.” Six days later, Reiner and his wife, Michelle Reiner, were stabbed to death in their home. Charged with murder, their son Nick Reiner has pleaded not guilty . Continue reading...

articles.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
articles.description: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Is Donald Trump beyond caricature? Not at all – here’s his hilarious origin story
articles.description: Ustinov Studio, Bath Elliot Cowan is scarily convincing as the budding Potus in Donald, a high-speed, three-actor comedy from the playwright behind The Lehman Trilogy His manner and actions often seeming like improbable caricature, the current US president sets a challenge for satire, any comic exaggeration likely to be trumped by reality. Mike Bartlett’s play The 47th (2022), staged between Trump’s administrations, pursued wild fantasies about the politician’s future career that were soon superseded by odder events. Ali Abbasi’s movie The Apprentice (2024) more sensibly focused on the period from 1973 to 1986 in which the New York realtor developed the behavioural and verbal tics that make him probably the most ridiculed figure in modern history, though such mockery, until the recent midterms, largely consoled detractors while being ignored by supporters. Closer to Abbasi’s approach, Donald by the Italian dramatist Stefano Massini resembles his play The Lehman Trilogy – an international hit about the banking dynasty – in being a psychological analysis played by three actors with lightning switches of character and costume. In this case, the cut-up structure reflects Massini’s seed

articles.title: ‘We can rage’: Michael Sheen fires up the gripping medieval epic Owain & Henry
articles.description: Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff Sheen is in wondrous voice as Owain Glyndŵr, clashing with Henry IV, in Gary Owen’s stirring history play for Welsh National Theatre No one does rousing like Michael Sheen. Whether urging on the Welsh World Cup squad or vowing “apocalypse” on The Traitors, he surges forward on waves of rhetoric. As Owain Glyndŵr, beacon of Welsh resistance, he doesn’t disappoint. “We can die gently and be forgotten,” he exhorts his followers. “Or we can rage .” Rage and resignation, the sword and the song, resonate through Gary Owen’s absorbing medieval epic for Wales Millennium Centre and Sheen’s new Welsh National Theatre . Glyndŵr is a marginal figure in Shakespeare’s Henry IV plays, a thorn in the unstable king’s side. Here he stands central, a fitting protagonist for a moment of both surging populist politics and a disillusionment with power play. Continue reading...

articles.title: Bet they look good on the dancefloor: Mark McNulty’s party people – in pictures
articles.description: If there was a rave going off in the 90s, one British photographer was likely there with his camera. His new book celebrates banging nights out at Cream, the Haçienda and more Continue reading...

articles.title: Walk, eat, sleep: 10 of the best hotels for ramblers in the UK and Ireland
articles.description: As the new Good Hotel Guide goes live online, the editors pick their favourite places to stay for hikers and strollers With stunning views over Borrowdale, Donna and Gary MacRae’s small country house hotel is in a walker’s wonderland, with routes for all abilities, from the challenge of a Wainwright to a stroll around the wooded grounds. Donna and Gary can supply a packed lunch, arrange for a mountain guide and share information on favourite walks. For Gary, that means a scenic, “easy-going stroll” from Dock Tarn to Watendlath National Trust village and tarn; for Donna, a hike to the top of Rigg Head Quarry, then on towards High Spy, along the river over Maiden Moor and Catbells. Drying facilities, drinks and canapes and a four-course dinner await the rovers’ return. Doubles from £ 200 B&B (2-night min) , dinner from £55pp, no pets, no under 15s, hazelbankhotel.co.uk Continue reading...

articles.title: Thursday news quiz: A hungry hippo, a distant Voyager and a new James Bond
articles.description: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare? The Thursday quiz spent the weekend up in Inverness where it was unexpectedly blinded by winter sunshine and met an awful lot of European herring gulls, including one particular persistent young chick that was quite adamant passersby should be feeding it. It clearly could not read the signs. Anyway, now is your opportunity to show you can read the signs, or at least read 15 questions on topical news, general knowledge and popular culture. There are no prizes except potentially a warm feeling inside. A considerably warmer feeling than Inverness at this time of year, at any rate. Allons-y! Continue reading...

articles.title: The Thanksgiving food traditions we could all share
articles.description: Warming pie, buttery mash and plenty of gravy are a perfect excuse to gather friends around the table during chilly November • Sign up here for our weekly food newsletter, Feast As a Brit, there are plenty of reasons for me not to embrace Thanksgiving, most of all because it isn’t actually a British holiday, and least of all because we already have quite enough occasions to eat ourselves silly between now and January. And yet, every November, as the days grow shorter and darker and colder, I find myself rather taken with the idea of hosting a seasonal dinner for friends. If Christmas is more formal and family-focused, then Thanksgiving feels like a prime opportunity to get pals around the table, eat until you need to undo your top trouser button, and take a moment to appreciate what you have. And if that means borrowing a few ideas from across the Atlantic – a warming spiced pumpkin pie , say, or a dish of fruity stuffing and a sharp cranberry sauce – well, there’s no reason we can’t make them our own. Obviously there are some crossovers with Britain’s main festive meal, turkey being the big one. Personally, I prefer to cook a cockerel on Christmas Day, which naturally gives me the

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for pasta all’arrabbiata with red onion and plums | A kitchen in Rome
articles.description: Much like tomato, the plum has a natural acidity and sweetness that works brilliantly in a delightfully jammy pasta sauce Standing on platform 2 at Baker Street station a few weeks ago, a grey creature scuttled under the raised tracks. “You’re never more than six feet away from a rat in London,” I said to my Roman son. “It’s a mouse, Mum,” was his hardboiled reply to my rehashing of an urban myth. A myth that turns out to be inaccurate, according to Dr David Cowan , whose research on the subject resulted in estimates of anything from 10ft-164ft: in other words, while it’s impossible to know for sure, in certain areas you might be very close to a rat. The same can be said about wild plum trees all over the world. articles.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
articles.description: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January . But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. articles.title: Country diary: A luminous morning of gig crews and green and gold foliage | Virginia Spiers
articles.description: Tamar Valley, Cornwall: In the autumn warmth, the river brings flotsam and Canada geese, while a group of vintage Austin car enthusiasts have a picnic By Cotehele quay, on the last of a sequence of calm sunlit days, thin plumes of mist rise from glistening mudbanks and reedbeds glow luminous in the morning sun. Gig crews drag their boats up the slipway, away from the ebbing water. Lime-loving old man’s beard on riverside bushes reminds us of the cargoes of limestone, once shipped with coal to these quays for burning in the monumental kilns. Upriver, the woodland path towards the river cliff chapel is strewn with dry leaves, and beech and sweet chestnut hang on to green and golden foliage. The National Trust’s valley garden remains in shade, apart from the fiery top of a swamp cypress , brilliant against the blue sky. Continue reading...

articles.description: Belfast Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme Training Exercise A training exercise to install the temporary defences will take place between 14 – 18 September 2026. articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.description: As part of an effort to keep Russia on the radar of African countries still struggling from some of the negative externalities of Russia’s continuing war in Ukraine, Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted African leaders in Moscow last week for the third Russia-Africa summit . Between October 28 and 29, Russian officials met with their African counterparts in high-level discussions covering a wide range of issues, primarily focused on continued security relations and opportunities for greater economic collaboration. Of course, Russian engagement with Africa isn’t new. The Russian paramilitary group Africa Corps has around 2,500 fighters on the continent, where it has formed relations with a number of African governments to fight armed groups in exchange for payment, including through access to commodities. The paramilitary group, which has committed human rights abuses and has largely failed to stop the spread of the armed group violence , has caused a souring of Russian goodwill in Africa. articles.title: Is Haiti becoming a front in a multinational conflict?
articles.description: On October 18, four Salvadoran airmen vanished after gunmen ambushed their armored vehicle in Croix-des-Bouquets, a gang-held suburb about seven kilometers outside Port-au-Prince, Haiti’s capital. They were in Haiti as part of a UN-authorized multinational force sent to retake territory from the armed gangs that now dominate large swathes of the Caribbean nation. El Salvador’s hardline president, Nayib Bukele, famous for jailing tens of thousands of suspected gang members at home without due process under a state of exception, insists his contingent was there for medical evacuations, “not to wage war.” Within days he rushed hundreds more troops to the island, reportedly now 2,500 , with U.S. C-130s helping fly them in. At the U.N. Security Council, U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz, calling Haiti a failed state, promised the missing men: “we will bring you home.” How did Salvadoran airmen end up in a gang ambush outside Port-au-Prince? Something has shifted in official messaging. Across Europe, the UK's "Be Ready" campaign is telling households to stock three days of water, food, cash, and a radio. The EU's Preparedness Union Strategy, rolled out last year and reinforced recently, aims for 72 hours of household self-sufficiency. Japan, several Nordic countries, and others have issued or updated similar guidance. In the United States, the Pentagon has directed bases toward greater self-sufficiency, and FEMA is running a nationwide Emergency Alert System test today. These are not brand-new ideas. Civil defense and household preparedness have long been sensible policy. What stands out is the clustering and the broader backdrop: geopolitical risks in Europe, the Middle East and elsewhere, hybrid threats, and infrastructure that keeps revealing its fragility. articles.title: The Ironies Of Stimulus, Recession, And The Conflagration To Come
articles.description: The Ironies Of Stimulus, Recession, And The Conflagration To Come Authored by Charles Hugh Smith via Of Two Minds , The conflagration that's now inevitable will only be made worse by pouring the gasoline of stimulus on the embers. For the past 45 years, the unspoken policy of the Federal Reserve and government has been to ward off recession with stimulus - lowering interest rates and easing credit to boost borrowing, and increasing federal spending. This is the Keynesian belief structure that has guided policy since the end of World War II 80 years ago: recessions are painful, so let's get rid of them . Why suffer defaults, insolvencies and layoffs when we could keep growth going with central bank and fiscal stimulus? This mindset, shaped by The Great Depression, viewed recessions as potential sources of self-reinforcing catastrophe: once the stock market fell and credit dried up, spending fell and as workers were laid off, the slowdown deepened as lower borrowing and spending led to more layoffs which further reduced borrowing and spending, with the eventual result being a Depression. articles.description: Every Airline Flight Is A Government Flight Authored by Matthew G. Andersson via American Thinker , The recent nation-wide airline ground stop that was ordered by the FAA under Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, should make it clear to airline passengers that you fly from one place to another at the pleasure of the government . Image: Grok, AI-generated illustration . This isn't an entirely bad thing, but it is important to understand that an "airline" is much more than the brand painted on the airplane. The airline industry is made up of what I've called the "five A's." They stand for the airline, the airport it flies from, the airspace it flies in, the air traffic control (ATC) that separates flights, and the agency, or Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that regulates it all. Outside of the particular airline you fly on, each one of those other components of the airline system is a government system , and government property. Some airports are owned by various state and municipal organizations, but they ultimately fall under federal authority. articles.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?
articles.description: Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days. The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Strangers gave me £2,409’: the online community helping people in debt
articles.description: People come together online to support one another with small voluntary donations to ease financial worries For some time people struggling with debt have used social media to document what they owe, swap advice and hold themselves accountable as they try to pay it off. Some have built large audiences around their repayment journeys, using views and engagement to generate income through creator payment schemes, livestream gifts and donations from followers towards their debts. Now the idea is being taken a step further: rather than one person building an audience to help clear their own debt, strangers are creating communities to help pay off one another’s. Continue reading...

articles.title: Naming your feelings can be harder than you think. This simple tool can help
articles.description: About 10% of people have significant trouble identifying their emotions – which makes it harder to know what to do about them Naming emotions is a core skill that most people develop as children, and it might seem like second nature. But research indicates that it’s harder than you think – about 10% of the general population have significant difficulty identifying their own emotions. That’s why a simple tool called the feelings wheel has gained popularity in therapists’ offices and classrooms over recent years. Continue reading...

articles.title: Quel head trip! Failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film rock Paris Photo – review
articles.description: Grand Palais, Paris The fair celebrated the bicentenary of photography – but did anyone care? Especially when the most compelling images proposed whole new ways of seeing No one at the three-day Paris Photo fair seemed worried about being a target for protesters – the fate of fellow art fair Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early. “Photography isn’t expensive enough,” joked one gallerist. This 29th edition coincided with celebrations across France of the bicentenary of photography, and as such looked back at photography’s origins and the questions that have preoccupied photographers from the beginning. One example was a 19th-century portrait that is thought to be an extremely rare depiction of Rimbaud with a black eye – the poet was a known ruffian who often got physical over literary squabbles. Whether the photograph is really Rimbaud or not begs the question: what matters more, the truth, or what we believe the truth to be? After 200 years, photography hasn’t resolved the issue. The strongest thread running through Paris Photo is the uncertainty and instability of photography: as evidence that collapses into fiction and performance. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘His wife was horrified’: did Edward Hopper paint his sexual problems?
articles.description: He is the maestro of American melancholy. But in a new biography, the artist is called a ‘sadist’ and a ‘prize hog’ by his wife – who was aghast to see their domestic and bedroom problems surface in his most famous works It should have been a happy occasion. In 1950, an Edward Hopper retrospective was staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York – but the artist’s wife, the painter Josephine (Jo) Nivison Hopper, was in a fury. The show’s catalogue, written by the museum’s director, had originally stated that in 1924 Edward “married the artist Josephine Nivison Hopper”, yet in the final version, the phrase “the artist” had been removed. “I’m not allowed to exist even in my husband’s biography,” Jo seethed in a private notebook that has just come to light. “And that’s all right with EH.” Due to her own strenuous efforts, Jo not only exists, but is a vital protagonist in my new biography of Edward Hopper. Jo once contemplated writing her husband’s biography herself, having amassed such an overwhelming body of material documenting their tumultuous marriage. As Edward’s creative partner, muse, curator, producer and unofficial manager, Jo produced 35 years’ worth of daily dia

articles.title: Simply telling the AA about my minor no-fault, no-claim prang doubled my insurance quote
articles.description: A recent £364 renewal quote suddenly increased to an extortionate £796 My car was involved in a minor no-fault accident. The other driver admitted responsibility and said they would pay for repairs without involving insurers. I informed my insurer, the AA, without making a claim. It had recently sent a renewal quote for £364, but after reporting the accident I was sent a revised figure of £796.86. I was told by a call handler that any insurance company would do the same. However, they eventually lowered the quote to £452.31. This seems extortionate for a no-fault, no-claim prang. Continue reading...

articles.title: Belonging by Sonia Gandhi review – India’s elder stateswoman breaks her silence
articles.description: The Italian who became kingmaker in the world’s largest democracy charts her remarkable journey By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history. No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years. Continue reading...

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the bedbugs that bit me – and worried Jake Gyllenhaal
articles.description: An infestation at my hotel meant my clothes had to be fumigated. When I turned up in shorts to interview the actor, he lent me his jacket, but I suspect he may have regretted it The biting flies were wild in Toronto in September 2012. A colleague and I were there to cover the film festival, but our key reference that year was a zinger from the 2007 cartoon Bee Movie, when it turns out Chris Rock’s mosquito has become a lawyer: “I was already a bloodsucking parasite,” he says, “all I needed was a briefcase!” (Bee Movie is one of the most brilliant and adult children’s movies ever; its central premise compares the honey industry to concentration camps.) Anyway, I spent the first week getting ever more bloodless and lumpy. We even shot a video about them, spraying repellent in front of us like Mace. It didn’t work. Every morning I woke bumpier than before. Continue reading...

articles.title: A heretical outrage: why Italians disown spaghetti bolognese
articles.description: Spag bol carries my city’s name all over the world – to the embarrassment of restaurants in Bologna In Bologna, spaghetti bolognese does not exist. You’ll find it on menus in London and Sydney, in British school canteens and in jars on supermarket shelves across half the world, but not in the city that lent it its name. Order it in a trattoria beneath the Two Towers and at best you get a pitying smile. More often you’ll be brought a plate of tagliatelle, with a short lesson in local history on the side. Few of the Italian dishes famous abroad carry the name of a city. Every so often the argument flares up again over where pizza, carbonara or tiramisu were born. With spaghetti bolognese the parentage is written into the name, and yet, absurdly, it is the Bolognese themselves who disown it. Many regard it as an outrage, a heretical and misshapen version cooked only by people who know nothing of real Bolognese food. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘She set out to buy a painting a day’: on the trail of Peggy Guggenheim’s legendary shopping spree
articles.description: Royal Academy, London The modernist collector once ran a gallery in London – but from this confusing exhibition, it’s hard to tell what exactly was once in there Peggy Guggenheim, art enthusiast and socialite born into a wealthy New York family, was often photographed outside her palazzo in Venice with a handbag dog and outré sunglasses. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection as we now know it, however, was nearly not in her Venice palazzo but London, evidenced by a short-lived and largely overlooked period between January 1938 and June 1939 when she ran Guggenheim Jeune in Cork Street. This exhibition posits that this initial gallery’s activities were far more influential in the shaping of contemporary art than previously recognised. Guggenheim Jeune mounted a flurry of 20 exhibitions including such UK firsts as a group show dedicated to collage, and solo exhibitions by Wassily Kandinsky , Jean Cocteau and Yves Tanguy . How to demonstrate the pioneering qualities of a gallery that is now a ghost? With reassembling and contextual padding, it appears. The catalogue states that at least 60% of the artworks in this exhibition were originally shown at Guggenheim Jeune, though only a handful o

articles.title: Help! Why does my apple pie always have a soggy base? | Kitchen aide
articles.description: Direct the heat and minimise the moisture to save your pastry from a saturated bottom, says our panel of pie pros Why does the pastry base of my apple pie always come out soggy? What am I doing wrong? Sophie, by email “The very first thing I would say is that Sophie has got to look at her filling, and how wet it is,” says Calum Franklin, author of The Modern Pie Maker and all-round pie Yoda. “Apples contain quite a lot of water already, so you don’t generally need to add any extra liquid to the filling.” Instead, he’d simply cook the apples with sugar: “Just let them break down.” That said, Sophie could always consider including some sort of barrier, too, says Dee Rettali, co-founder of Fortitude Bakehouse in London: “My mother was an amazing baker, and she always sprinkled a very fine crumble mix [just sugar and flour, no fat] on the bottom of her pie before putting in any fruit. That will then absorb most of the liquid.” Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com Continue reading...

articles.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.description: With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south. Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions. Continue reading...

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tell us: did you move to the countryside for retirement and come to regret it?
articles.description: As England’s chief medical officer warns of the challenges of growing older in rural areas, we’d like to hear from people who have struggled with isolation or accessing services and support England’s chief medical officer Chris Whitty has warned of the potential downsides of choosing to spend the later part of your life in a rural area. He urged people to think carefully about the challenges of rural life as they get older, including poor access to healthcare, limited public transport and the risk of becoming isolated or dependent on others. We want to hear from the people people who have experienced these challenges. Did you move to the countryside for your retirement and find it more difficult to access the services and support you need? Are you feeling dependent on others to get around and access amenities, leaving you wishing you’d stayed in a town or city? Or have you moved back to a city, finding rural life too isolating as you become older? Continue reading...

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone

On the call, organizers from Ready for AOC, a new group of progressive and labor organizers, wasted little time celebrating the Democrats’ electoral sweep. “People all over the country are ready for a much different and much better future,” said Genevieve Rand, an organizer with the group. “We are more ready than we have ever been.” Continue reading...

This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but. articles.title: Childhood neglect, unmet needs, mental health struggles: this is the making of a Neet | Mark Mon-Williams
articles.description: As a researcher for the Milburn review, I’ve seen how we’ve failed a generation – then castigated them. Britain must break this vicious cycle Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term prosperity if we just keep patching over these symptoms. The solution to any problem starts with understanding its causes, and Milburn and Fonagy provide a thoughtful analysis. I have worked closely with both of them, being a topic group member for Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, and supporting Milburn with data analytics. Their reviews have followed the evidence, all of which shows a system neglecting children at scale. We have decreased benefits and slashed the support provided to children: today 4.5 million children are living in poverty. When these children grow up and are diagnosed with anxie

articles.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
articles.description: After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI . But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes. Continue reading...

articles.title: After 49 years, Nasa’s Voyager 1 is one light-day away from us. Can we save this ‘pale blue dot’? | Kim Heacox
articles.description: Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering. Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home. Continue reading...

articles.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description: The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while , and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down. Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire . I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company , Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m). Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The aesthetics in my family were so high, I felt ugly’: Charlotte Gainsbourg on extremism, abortion and her mother, Jane Birkin
articles.description: In her new film, the actor plays a lawyer taking on the French state over reproductive rights. She talks about being criticised for her support of Israel and pushed to the limit by Lars von Trier While she was making the film Women on Trial , about the real-life trial of a child prosecuted for having an abortion, someone sent Charlotte Gainsbourg a photograph of her mother at one of the pro-choice demonstrations that erupted in France at the time. It was “very moving”, says Gainsbourg to see her mother, the actor Jane Birkin, in 1972, “looking beautiful and in the middle of a demonstration”. At that time, in a court in Bobigny, a Paris suburb, the prominent lawyer Gisèle Halimi was defending 16-year-old Marie-Claire Chevalier, as well as her mother and two other women who helped her have an abortion, then illegal in France. The Bobigny trial was new to her, says Gainsbourg, who plays Halimi, a leading figure in French feminism and activism who died in 2020. “I had no idea. For me, abortion rights started with Simone Veil” – the French minister of health who saw through decriminalisation three years later – “so I had to catch up.” Continue reading...

articles.title: From Dumb Starbucks to dada documentary: everything you need to know about Nathan Fielder
articles.description: With the UK release of You Can See Everything looming, now’s an ideal time to get up to speed on the bizarre, puckish and very meta comedic oeuvre of its star “There are three sides to every story: your side, my side, and the truth. And no one is lying. Memories shared serve each differently.” Those words were spoken by film producer Robert Evans – but nobody has ever interrogated the idea more skilfully than comedian Nathan Fielder. The three-hour documentary You Can See Everything – co-directed by and starring Fielder – opens in the UK on Friday, having already become an unlikely cultural phenomenon and box office sensation in the US. The film follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her beginning a prison sentence for defrauding investors; what emerges is a profound meditation on the nature of truth and the fundamental unknowability of other human beings. To view the film as being simply about the Theranos scandal is akin to considering Casablanca merely a movie about a nightclub. And, as one might expect given Fielder’s background, it’s hilarious. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ta-Nehisi Coates on the shocking case that shattered his childhood and inspired new HBO documentary
articles.description: A 36-year fight for justice is explored in the galling HBO documentary When a Witness Recants. The three subjects and producer Coates explain how it unfolded For most of his life, the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates would occasionally think of a chilling episode from his childhood in West Baltimore: almost exactly 43 years ago, on 18 November 1983, a 14-year-old boy named DeWitt Duckett was shot and killed in a hallway of Harlem Park junior high school in the middle of the afternoon, by an older teenager who stole his blue satin Georgetown jacket. Coates was only eight at the time, too young to know the details, but old enough to perceive the collective horror around him. The sensational event – the first time a kid was killed inside a Baltimore public school, according to wall-to-wall local press – was a rupture in his child’s view of the world. “It was first time I had the sense that, oh, actually, I exist in a very dangerous world,” he told the Guardian. “And then you cut to the TV and it’s clear the rest of America is not existing in that dangerous world. The dangerous world is only for you and people who look like you.” Coates always assumed that the three teenage boys arrested and co

articles.title: Prawn masala and spiced roast cauliflower: Romy Gill’s Indian recipes for chilly nights
articles.description: Spiced prawns cooked in coconut milk and a whole roast cauliflower with almonds and coriander – these dishes take me back to the food of my childhood These two dishes are just the kind of food I want to eat on a chilly evening. The cauliflower is deeply spiced, nutty and comforting, with coconut, almonds, ginger and chilli bringing warmth and texture, while the prawn masala is quicker and lighter, but still full of flavour, with the spices and the sweet prawns coming together beautifully. Both dishes reflect the way I love to cook: generous, vibrant with layers of spice, but never so much that you lose the character of the main ingredient. Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: Thrilling views of Iceland’s humpbacks, (perhaps) lured in by Céline Dion | Claire Stares
articles.description: Eyjafjörður: Our boat was surrounded by around 15 of them, exploding their exhalations out of the water – and numbers are increasing here For the first half-hour, Eyjafjörður, Iceland’s longest fjord, offered few signs of marine life – just three cormorants and a raft of common eiders. Then, suddenly, there it was. A distant spout of water vapour. A  humpback whale . As we motored out, more bushy plumes appeared to port and starboard, until we found the boat surrounded by about 15 individuals. Cutting the engine, the captain announced that he was about to employ a secret technique to coax the whales closer. There were raised eyebrows as the opening notes of Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On crackled over the speakers. But, as if on cue, two explosive exhalations erupted alongside the boat, prompting whoops of delight. Continue reading...

articles.description: The Prince and Princess of Wales met the prime minister of India on Wednesday to discuss trade and bilateral ‌ties at the end of their three-day visit to the country.
